blocks.text: III. The third name of the locust, גזם gazam, Ioel I, 4. and II, 25. and Amos IV, 9., the Hebrews derive from גוז guz or גזז gazaz, which means to shear and to cut off. And they hold that the final Mem is servile, although they produce no similar noun. For חנם, gratis [freely], ריקם, frustra [in vain], דומם, quiete [quietly], יומם, interdiu [by day], אמנם, vere [truly], which they cite here, are not nouns but adverbs. Therefore the true root is the verb גזם gazam, which the Talmudists sometimes use in the sense of cutting off and pruning: as in Avoda Zara fol. 50 b, אין מגזמין וסכין שמן בגזום, They do not prune the branches of trees, but they smear oil on the place of the pruning. So in Arabic, in Alcamus, جَزَمَ النحل [jazama al-nakhl], He pruned the palm. In Ethiopic too it occurs for ἐκκόπτειν [ekkoptein], Matth. III, 10. and VII, 19. Luc. III, 9. and XIII, 7. 9. In these places too the subject is the cutting down of trees. From this, then, locusts were named, because with their very sharp teeth they gnaw not only grass, crops and the leaves of trees, but also the bark and the more tender twigs of the trees themselves, as if they were cutting them off. Pliny, in the place cited above: Scorching many things by their touch, but gnawing everything with their bite, even the doors of houses. Jerome on Joel ch. 1: The Jews think that in the days of Joel so innumerable a multitude of locusts came upon Judaea that they filled everything, and left, I will not say the crops, but not even the bark and branches of the vines and trees. And also Amos IV, 9.: Your gardens, and your vineyards, and your fig groves, and your olive groves יאכל הגזם, the Gazam (or locust) shall eat. Accordingly [col. 444] Pisides attributes to the swarms of locusts a μυριόστομον ξίφος [myriostomon xiphos], a sword of ten thousand edges. So much according to the mind of the Hebrews, who with the greatest agreement hold that גזם gazam is a species of locust: following, of course, the Chaldee, for whom gazam is זחלא, the creeping locust, [III, 254] or ἄπτερος [apteros], as we shall show below. The Syriac also renders it ܡܫܘܛܐ in the same sense. For ܡܫܘܛܐ is the Chaldee שמוטא inverted. And שמוטא is counted among the species of locust, as is the Hebrew חסיל, for which it stands in Jonathan on 1 Reg. VIII, 37. and Ioel. I, 4. ^{(3)}. But for the Greeks and Jerome גזם gazam is κάμπη [kampē], caterpillar. Although Fuller in his Miscellanea, book 5, ch. 20, tries to defend this version with many arguments, he by no means persuades me: both because the Hebrews, Chaldeans and Syrians think otherwise, and because the name גזם gazam, formed from the pruning of branches, seems to suit the caterpillar less than the locust, whose bite is stronger. For the bite of the caterpillar scorches rather than cuts off. Columella:
— — — and the caterpillar creeps through the gardens, And, advancing over them, scorches the seedlings with its bite.

Therefore, just as it is called ERUCA from gnawing [erodere], so it is also called URUCA from burning [urere]. The old Latin-Greek Glosses edited by Stephanus, p. 347: Uruca, κάμπη [kampē]. And the Greek-Latin ones, p. 501: Κάμπη λαχάνου [Kampē lachanou], Eruca, uruca. And p. 516: Λαχάνων κάμπη [Lachanōn kampē], urica. Since these three places confirm one another, none of them ought to have been suspect to Fuller ^{(4)}.

IV. Aben Ezra on Leviticus asserts that the fourth name of the locust, חגב chagab, is known מלשון ישמעאל, from the language of Ishmael, that is, Arabic: which is utterly false. For although among the Arabs there are very many names for locusts, none similar to this one occurs. Yet the origin of the word may be Arabic. For [III, 255] the Arabic verb حجب [ḥajaba] chagaba means to veil. Thus Avicenna, in the chapter On the anatomy of the eye, teaches that the ἀραχνοειδῆν [arachnoeidēn] tunic is thin for this reason, that if it were dense, يحجب الضو عن الجليدية [yaḥjub al-ḍaw ʿan al-jalīdiyya] it would veil the light from the glacial humour, or crystalline, that is, it would keep the light from it as if by a veil spread before it. Hence حجاب [ḥijāb] chigab is the veil, Matth. XXVII, 51. and Hebr. VI, 19., and حاجب [ḥājib] chagib, that is, doorkeeper, Gen. XLIII, 16. 19. in the Paris edition; because in closing the door he as it were draws a veil over it. I would therefore think that locusts were called חגבים chagabim from the same source, because when they fly in swarms they seem to draw a veil over the light of the sun, as we shall show below on Ioel. II, 20. ^{(5)}.
